lesson.title: Multiplying Across a Sum: The Distributive Property
lesson.summary: Explains the distributive property, a(b + c) = ab + ac, as the rule that lets a single factor multiply every term inside parentheses, verified with both numeric and algebraic examples.
lesson.body:
The distributive property connects multiplication and addition by stating that a(b + c) equals ab + ac. In words, when a number multiplies a sum inside parentheses, that number must multiply every single term inside the parentheses separately, and then you add the resulting products together. This property is what allows you to remove parentheses from an expression like 3(x + 4) and rewrite it as 3x + 12, a move you will use constantly once you start simplifying and solving more complicated expressions and equations.

You can verify the distributive property is true using ordinary arithmetic before trusting it with variables. Take 3(4 + 5). Following order of operations normally, you would add first: 4 + 5 = 9, then multiply: 3 times 9 = 27. Now distribute instead: 3(4) + 3(5) = 12 + 15 = 27. Both methods land on 27, confirming that distributing the 3 across the sum before adding gives the identical result to adding first and multiplying second. This works for any numbers, which is exactly why it is promoted to a general property rather than treated as a coincidence.

The real value of the distributive property shows up once a variable sits inside the parentheses, because at that point you can no longer add the terms together first the way you did with plain numbers; the variable's value is not known, so distributing is the only way forward. Consider 5(x + 3). You cannot simplify x + 3 any further since x and 3 are not like terms, so distribute the 5 across both terms: 5(x) + 5(3) = 5x + 15. This is now a simplified expression with two terms, a coefficient attached to a variable and a constant, exactly the vocabulary built up earlier in this chapter.

The distributive property also works when the term inside the parentheses is being subtracted, and when the outside multiplier is negative, both of which require careful attention to signs. Let's work through negative 4(2x minus 7). Distribute the negative 4 across both terms inside the parentheses: negative 4 times 2x, plus negative 4 times negative 7. The first product is negative 8x. The second product multiplies two negative numbers, which gives a positive result: negative 4 times negative 7 = 28. So the expression becomes negative 8x + 28. Check this by evaluating both the original and distributed versions at x = 3. Original: negative 4(2(3) minus 7) = negative 4(6 minus 7) = negative 4(negative 1) = 4. Distributed: negative 8(3) + 28 = negative 24 + 28 = 4. Both give 4, confirming the distribution was carried out correctly, signs and all.

Distributing is also what allows you to combine like terms hiding inside separate sets of parentheses, since once every parenthesis is expanded, everything becomes a flat list of terms that the commutative and associative properties can freely rearrange and regroup, ready for like terms to be combined the way you practiced earlier.
